name: Ninkyop / Ninkyob
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 3 other works consulted do not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Blench, Roger & Hauwa Kadima. 2011 [printout 19 Oct 2011; fieldwork 3-5 Nov 2005]. The Ninkyop language of Central Nigeria and its affinities. Draft circulated for comment. Cambridge: Kay Williamson Educational Foundation. 34 pp. (= Glottolog ref 55674 'Blench 2006', listed by Glottolog as a wordlist; from archived copy (Internet Archive, 2024) of rogerblench.info)
catalog_quote: 3.3 Tones The tone system of Ninkyop is complex due to morphophonemic alternations. The underlying system has three tone heights, e.g. zíg row of ridges / zig knife / zìŋ giving gift. There is also a rising tone; yǔŋ love / ᶆwǐ ground / ɣwǒm old person and a falling tone; ᶆwârr joy / nʒôrɲ horn / ngû feather. The falling tone is much rarer than the rising tone. A low-mid tone that occurs only in words of two syllables or more. Examples; ǹjɔ᷅r evening / nshi᷅d tick / nyúŋʒyɛ᷅ animal
world_status: accessible description is silent on stress

new_statements.rule_in_words: Ninkyop (Kaninkon) is described as a tone language with three underlying level tone heights (high, mid, low) plus rising, falling and a low-mid contour; tone is lexically contrastive on monosyllables (zíg / zig / zìŋ) and raised as a plural-marking process. The source says nothing at all about word stress or accent, so no stress placement can be read from it.
new_statements.exceptions: None stated regarding stress; the tone description notes that the falling tone is rare and the low-mid tone occurs only in words of two or more syllables.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level lexical tone illustrated on citation-form nouns and verbs (mostly monosyllabic roots); the source is an annotated wordlist based on three days of fieldwork (2005) and the unpublished Kadima & Jerzyk phonology; draft 'not for citation without reference to the authors'.
new_statements.identity_note: The one opened description (Blench & Kadima 2011) covers Ninkyop = Ninkyob = Kaningkom/Kaninkon/Kaninkwom, i.e. the Kaningdom dialect kani1278 of kani1277 (villages Bakin Kogi, Gerti, Amere; Turan / Mbeco / Nkpa Nkun pronunciations), not Nindem (nind1241), for which no description of any kind was found. The two Ilorin theses (Kaninkon / Kaningkon) also concern the Ninkyob side.

tone_statements.citation: Kempton, Timothy. 2020. Proposals for a tone orthography of Nikyob following a participatory workshop. In Eno-Abasi Urua, Francis Egbokhare, Oluseye Adesola & Harrison Adeniyi (eds.), African Languages in Time and Space: A Festschrift in Honour of Professor Akinbiyi Akinlabi, pp. 48-70. Ibadan (Ashi, Bodija): Zenith BookHouse. ISBN 978-978-980-971-4. [Online version with audio:https://speechchemistry.github.io/faa/nikyob_tone; PDF in SIL Language and Culture Archives (REAP).]
tone_statements.quote: In isolated words there appears to be three level tones: low, mid and high which can be labelled with the Chao tone letters [˩ ˧ ˥]. There are also tone contours: low-mid rise, mid-low falling and high-mid falling which can be labelled [˩˧ ˧˩ ˥˧]. [...] There appears to be three contrastive level tones in isolation forms. One possible interpretation of the patterns observed at the workshop is that there are just two underlying tones in Nikyob but more than two realizations of these tones in the speech of people. These realizations or surface tones arise through processes called downstep and upstep.

tone_statements.n_tones: 3 surface level tones (L, M, H) + 3-4 contours; possibly 2 underlying (L, H) pe…
tone_statements.summary: 3 surface level tones L/M/H + LM, ML, HM contours (HL on past-tense verbs); possibly 2 underlying tones with non-automatic downstep and upstep; heavy grammatical tone (noun number, person of pronouns, tense); no stress statement.

tone_statements.citation: Blench, Roger & Hauwa Kadima. 2011 [printout 19 October 2011]. Ninkyob ideophones. Draft circulated for comment. Cambridge: Kay Williamson Educational Foundation. 16 pp. (PDF on the author's site, Ninzic/Ninkyop directory; the Internet Archive capture 2024-07-24.)
tone_statements.quote: Ninkyob normally has three contrastive tone heights; zíg row of ridges zig knife zìŋ giving gift as well as rising and falling tones composed of glides between different tone levels. However, ideophones have only two tone heights, low and high, illustrated by the contrastive pairs typical of the repertoire. gbáŋ describes s.t far away gbàŋ describes s.t. high up such as the top of a tree ... True rising and falling tones occur, but they are extremely rare (<2%) of the basic repertoire, although they occur in extended forms of glissando tones;
tone_statements.summary: Three contrastive tone heights (third height unnamed, unmarked) plus rising/falling glides composed of levels; ideophones use only high and low, some with glissandi. Nothing on stress or TBU.
